records.summary: DLA Energy awarded Doyon Utilities a utility privatization contract on 2007-09-28 covering Army installation utility systems in Alaska, with a period of performance that runs to 2058-08-14 — a fifty-one year term. The award record shows $894,733,810 already obligated and a base-and-all-options value of $3,082,072,958, making this by a wide margin the largest single utility vehicle surfaced in this sweep. A companion contract to the same recipient on the same day (SP0600-07-C-8261) carries a further $212,665,748 obligated. The contractor is a regulated utility: its rates at these installations are set by the Regulatory Commission of Alaska, not by the contract alone.
records.microreactor_read: This is the instrument a microreactor should be sold into rather than around: a single counterparty already holds a fifty-year, three-billion-dollar franchise to supply heat and power to Alaska Army installations, and its generation is coal and oil in a place where fuel arrives by rail and barge. The reactor does not need to beat a $/kW number to enter — it needs to become an asset inside a rate base a regulator already approves, and the addressable line is the roughly $60M a year of obligations this one contract has averaged since 2007.

records.summary: NAVFAC EXWC issued Ameresco a task order under the DOE ESPC IDIQ on 2016-12-28 to build and then operate a site-wide microgrid at Marine Corps Recruit Depot Parris Island, with a period of performance running to 2041-11-30. Ameresco announced the deal as a $91.1 million self-funding ESPC covering 10 MW of new on-site generation, a 3.5 MW gas CHP plant replacing the end-of-life steam plant, 6.7 MW-DC of solar PV and an 8.0 MWh battery. The federal award record tells a different story about size: $66,631,952 has been obligated so far and the contract's base-and-all-options value is $212,716,674 — 2.3x the announced $91.1M, because the ESPC's later years are performance-period service payments, not construction. The host pays nothing up front and repays out of guaranteed savings across roughly 25 years.
records.microreactor_read: Two numbers matter to a microreactor seller here and they are far apart: the capital comparison is $91.1M for about 10 MW of mixed generation, i.e. roughly $9,100/kW nameplate and about $26,000/kW if you count only the 3.5 MW of firm dispatchable CHP; the commercial comparison is the $212.7M of lifecycle contract value a 25-year vehicle at one recruit depot can actually carry. A 5-10 MW microreactor priced against the $91.1M sticker looks expensive and priced against the $212.7M lifecycle envelope looks financeable — which is why the instrument, not the capex, is the thing to copy.

records.summary: In July 2019 NAVFAC Southeast awarded Siemens Government Technologies an ESPC task order — announced at $828.8 million and issued for 25 years of construction plus operation — to replace diesel generation at Naval Station Guantanamo Bay with a dual-fuel LNG combined-cycle plant and a solar field. The plant was commissioned on 2023-09-07 and is rated 20 MW; the plant alone cost $368.8 million. The federal award record shows $101,059,504 obligated so far against a base-and-all-options value of $927,391,394 with a potential end date of 2043-04-24, so the contract has grown roughly $100M past its announced value and only about 11 percent of the ceiling has been obligated. The 15 pre-existing diesel generators were not retired; they were kept for outages and peaks.
records.microreactor_read: Guantanamo is the strongest capex-per-MW argument in this file and it runs the reactor's way: $368.8M for 20 MW of island generation is $18,440/kW, and that is for a gas plant whose fuel still has to arrive by ship. A 1-20 MW microreactor competing at an isolated base does not need to beat $5,400/kW — at a site with no pipeline and no grid tie it needs to beat roughly $18,000/kW plus a fuel logistics chain, against a counterfactual the Navy itself valued at $24.6M a year in savings over 22 years.

records.summary: The Regulatory Commission of Alaska set the FY2024 Power Cost Equalization base rate at $0.1935/kWh on 13 June 2023 and, a week later, recalculated the per-kWh PCE credit for every participating rural utility. The attached Appendix 1 sheets are the single best published price-to-beat dataset in US remote power: for each utility they state test-period kWh sales, non-fuel power cost per kWh, fuel/purchased-power cost per kWh, and total power cost per kWh. Total power costs run from about $0.41/kWh at wind-equipped Kotzebue to $1.9487/kWh at Lime Village, with fuel alone above $0.81/kWh at Igiugig and $1.52/kWh at Lime Village. The state pays the gap above the base rate up to a statutory ceiling of $1.00/kWh of total cost, so any community whose costs exceed roughly $1.00/kWh is already eating unsubsidised cost.
records.microreactor_read: This is the price sheet. A 1-20 MW reactor selling into rural Alaska must beat a delivered cost of service that the regulator itself certifies at $0.62-$1.95/kWh, with the fuel-only component alone at $0.38-$1.53/kWh in the villages - but the loads are tiny (Igiugig 272 MWh/yr, Kokhanok 359 MWh/yr), so only aggregated or hub communities like Kotzebue (19.7 GWh/yr, and already down at $0.41/kWh because of wind) present a load a reactor could actually serve. The commercially interesting band is the mid-size hub at $0.60-$1.00/kWh, not the cheapest and not the smallest.

parties.host: Department of the Air Force / 354th Fighter Wing

records.summary: On 11 June 2025 the Defense Logistics Agency Energy, acting for the Department of the Air Force, issued a Notice of Intent to Award to Oklo for the DoD's first commercial microreactor. The structure is a build-own-operate arrangement: Oklo would design, construct, own and operate the plant and sell electricity and steam to the base under a long-term, firm-fixed-price power purchase agreement reported at 30 years. Capacity is up to 5 MWe, sitting alongside Eielson's existing 23 MW coal-fired plant. No price has been published; the rate for power is explicitly left to contract negotiation, and the award is contingent on Oklo obtaining an NRC licence.
records.microreactor_read: This is the cleanest template for selling a 1-20 MW reactor into a remote outpost: the host buys energy, not a reactor, on a 30-year firm-fixed-price PPA from a private owner-operator, contracted by a central buying agency (DLA Energy) rather than the base. The commercially important gap is that no price is published, so the deal proves the instrument exists but sets no benchmark - and the reactor is sized at 5 MW against a 23 MW incumbent, i.e. it is a supplement, not a replacement.

records.summary: In June 2022 the DoD's Strategic Capabilities Office selected BWXT Advanced Technologies to build the Project Pele transportable microreactor prototype under a cost-type contract worth approximately $300 million depending on options. The unit is a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor rated 1 to 5 MWe, packaged into 20-foot ISO-compliant CONEX containers, designed to reach operation within 72 hours of on-site assembly and to be removed in under seven days. Core fabrication began in 2025 and the unit is expected to produce electricity at Idaho National Laboratory in 2028, roughly four years later than the original 2024 delivery target.
records.microreactor_read: Pele prices the first-of-a-kind transportable microreactor at roughly $300 million for 1-5 MWe, i.e. $60-300 million per MW - one to two orders of magnitude above anything a remote community pays. It is a capability purchase, not an energy purchase, and it is the number a commercial microreactor pitch has to explicitly distance itself from: Pele proves transportability and the DoD's willingness to fund it, and simultaneously proves that prototype economics do not touch even the $1.95/kWh worst-case rural Alaska cost of service.

records.summary: The single most useful disclosure in this sector. TUGLIQ's federally funded completion report for the Raglan wind-storage pilot states the northern power price band outright: rates range from $1.20/kWh at the high end to $0.20/kWh at the low end, and industrial self-generators - i.e. mines running their own diesel plants - average $0.25 to $0.60/kWh even with grouped purchasing. Against that, a C$20 million, 3 MW turbine with flywheel, lithium and hydrogen storage was projected to return C$41 million in fuel and O&M savings over 20 years at a mine burning ~60 million litres of diesel a year. Ottawa funded C$7.8 million of the pilot and returned with C$3.9 million and a further C$7.1 million for the Raglan 2.0 expansion.
records.microreactor_read: This is the number to beat, from a Government of Canada report rather than a vendor deck: $0.25-$0.60/kWh for an industrial self-generator in the Canadian North, with the tail up to $1.20/kWh. A 5 MW microreactor selling at even $0.30/kWh into a Raglan-class site clears the low end of that band, and the Raglan precedent shows the miner will let a third party own the asset and take federal money to de-risk the first unit. The binding constraint is not price - it is that Raglan's own report frames micro-grid collapse (ventilation loss at -40C) as the reason northern operators distrust new generation, so a reactor must prove it firms the grid rather than adding a new failure mode.

filings.type: NuScale Power Corp Form 8-K exhibit (KGHM press release)

records.summary: The only mining company anywhere to have taken a nuclear project through a national administrative permit. KGHM - a copper miner that also runs smelters and refineries - signed with NuScale in February 2022, executed a Task Order and Statement of Commencement under an Early Works Agreement in September 2022 at the Karpacz Economic Forum, applied to Poland's National Atomic Energy Agency for a 462 MWe six-module plant, and received the decision-in-principle in July 2023, the first step in Poland's permit chain for nuclear facilities. KGHM publicly denied reports in November 2023 that NuScale had terminated the arrangement. No construction contract or price has been published.
records.microreactor_read: The instructive part is the size: the miner that actually went nuclear specified 462 MWe, not 5 or 20, because its load is smelting and refining rather than a mill on a diesel microgrid. Mineral processing - not mining - is where the megawatts are, and it is usually grid-connected, so the reactor competes against a wholesale tariff rather than the $0.25-$0.60/kWh diesel band. For a 1-20 MW unit the read is negative on this precedent and positive on the pattern: process heat and refinery load justify nuclear at a miner's board, while a pit and a mill alone have not yet done so anywhere.

records.summary: The Canadian federal government has already sized this market and published the price. NRCan counts 24 current and potential off-grid mines in Canada suitable for SMR deployment, puts a first-of-a-kind 20 MWe mining SMR at C$200-350 million, and claims a 20-60% LCOE advantage over diesel. A 20 MWe unit at 90% capacity factor sells ~158 GWh/yr, so at the $0.35/kWh midpoint of the industrial self-generation band it grosses ~C$55m/yr - the FOAK capital is recovered inside a decade only if the site actually runs at that price and that load factor. The market is 24 sites, not hundreds, and NRCan names it.

records.summary: The direct competitor to a microreactor at Canada's most diesel-exposed mines is a wire, and it is priced. Nunavut's minister responsible for Qulliq Energy told the legislature in June 2025 that the Kivalliq Hydro-Fibre Link now costs an estimated C$3.2 billion, up from C$1.2 billion in 2019, for a 1,200 km line from Gillam, Manitoba to five Kivalliq communities, completion pushed to 2032. Agnico Eagle and the Inuit-owned proponent Nukik signed an MOU to work through the technical case and formalise commercial discussions. Meadowbank alone burns about 33.5 million litres of diesel a year - the mine is the anchor load that makes the line bankable.
records.microreactor_read: The reactor's competitor at Meadowbank and Meliadine is a C$3.2 billion wire that does not arrive until 2032 - and the mine, at about 33.5 of the 44.5 million litres of displaced diesel, is three-quarters of its justification. Priced against NRCan's C$200-350m for a 20 MWe mining SMR, a handful of on-site units would cover the mine's load for a small fraction of the line's cost and years sooner. What the reactor cannot buy is the rest of the package: the line also takes five Inuit communities off diesel under Inuit ownership, which is what is actually mobilising the public money.

records.summary: California's Standardized Regulatory Impact Assessment for the At-Berth Regulation is the rare document that puts a defensible dollar figure on port electrification. But the price to beat is brutal: $81M for 14 MW is ~$5,800/kW installed for a machine whose fuel is free digester gas, so a reactor has to sell against the remaining grid-supplied two-thirds of load, not against the CHP.

records.microreactor_read: This is the template contract for civic microreactor sales: a county with no capital budget, an asset owned by a third party for 25 years, and an energy services payment out of the operating line. records.name: Sterling Municipal Light Department battery storage backing the town police station and dispatch centre

parties.host: Town of Sterling / Sterling Municipal Light Department
parties.provider: NEC Energy Solutions (batteries); DOE Office of Electricity and Sandia National Laboratories provided technical support

records.capacity: 2 MW / 3.9 MWh battery at the Chocksett Road substation, paired with existing solar; islands to give up to 12 days of backup power to the police station and dispatch centre
records.capex: About $2.7 million total, of which a $1.46 million Massachusetts DOER resiliency grant and a $250,000 US Department of Energy grant
records.displaced: Peak demand and capacity charges: projected to save SMLD customers over $400,000 a year; Sandia calculated payback in fewer than seven years
records.summary: Sterling, a town of about 7,800 with its own municipal light department, installed the state's first utility-scale battery in 2016: 2 MW / 3.9 MWh from NEC Energy Solutions at the Chocksett Road substation, for roughly $2.7 million with a $1.46 million DOER resiliency grant and $250,000 from DOE. The system pays for itself on peak shaving - Sandia National Laboratories calculated payback under seven years and SMLD projects over $400,000 a year of customer savings - while the resilience benefit is that it can island with existing solar and carry the town's police station and 911 dispatch centre for up to 12 days.
records.microreactor_read: The entire critical civic load of a New England town - police station plus PSAP dispatch - is small enough that 3.9 MWh of batteries covers it for twelve days, and the economics were carried by peak shaving, not by resilience. A microreactor has no addressable product at this scale; the only civic entry point is the municipal utility itself, which buys on payback-under-seven-years arithmetic.
